A positive test is a clue, not the final answer.

Actual tells us whether a person really has flu; the test predicts positive (+) or negative (−). Even an accurate test can produce many false alarms when flu is rare.

Why balance matters. When flu is more common, more positive tests come from people who really have flu.

With the signal sensitivity and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

How this demonstration works

1,000 weighted people. Counts are expected values and may be fractional. Sick portion changes counts and precision; TPR and FPR stay fixed at the same signal sensitivity and score separation.

A CLOSER LOOK

You tested positive. What is the chance you really have the flu?
Simple view
The basics
Formulas
Bayes
A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 500 have the flu (yielding 480 true catches) and 500 are healthy (yielding 20 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 480 out of all 500 positive tests (96%).

See the step-by-step Bayes proof →

After Test + · Precision
Likelihood Ratio (LR+ = TPR ÷ FPR): 24× · How strongly a Test + boosts the odds of flu
TPR

If a person really has the flu, what is the chance the test catches it?

P(test + | flu) · Row rate · Fixed when sick portion changes

FPR
4%

If a person does NOT have the flu, what is the chance of a false alarm?

P(test + | no flu) · Row rate · Fixed when sick portion changes

Precision
96%

If a person gets a positive test (Test +), what is the chance they truly have the flu?

P(flu | test +) · Column rate · Changes with sick portion

Four possible outcomes (2×2 Confusion Matrix)
1,000 weighted people · arranged in the exact same 2×2 positions as the matrix above
Top-left · Sick, Test −
FN · 20
Flu missed: person really has the flu, but the test came back negative (Test −).
Top-right · Sick, Test +
TP · 480
Flu caught: person really has the flu, and the test came back positive (Test +).
Bottom-left · Healthy, Test −
TN · 480
Correctly cleared: person does not have the flu, and the test came back negative (Test −).
Bottom-right · Healthy, Test +
FP · 20
False alarm: person does not have the flu, yet the test came back positive (Test +).

Why a rare disease creates mostly false alarms. When flu is rare (say 10% sick), 900 out of 1,000 people are healthy. Even a small 4% false-alarm rate on 900 healthy people creates 36 false alarms—diluting the 96 true catches down to 72.7% Precision.

With the signal sensitivity and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

How this demonstration works

1,000 weighted people. Counts are expected values and may be fractional. Sick portion changes counts and precision; TPR and FPR stay fixed at the same signal sensitivity and score separation.

EQUATIONS
THEORY
Click any metric card in Values to jump here. These are the standard formulas written in the usual notation.
TPR (RECALL)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
TPR = TP / (TP + FN)
Also written as: Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
Among the actual positives, what fraction did the model catch?
FPR
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
FPR = FP / (FP + TN)
Also written as: FPR = 1 - TNR
Among the actual negatives, what fraction were wrongly predicted positive?
PRECISION (PPV)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Also written as: PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Among the predicted positives, what fraction are truly positive?
ACCURACY
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
Also written as: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / N
Out of all predictions, what fraction were correct?
F1 SCORE
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
Also written as: F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall)
A balanced score that gets high only when both precision and recall are high.
AUC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
AUC = ∫01 TPR(FPR) d(FPR)
Also written as: area under the ROC curve
It summarizes performance across all thresholds, not just the current one.
NPV
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
NPV = negative predictive value
Among the predicted negatives, what fraction are truly negative?
MCC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
MCC = (TP · TN - FP · FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
Range: -1 to 1
Uses all four confusion-matrix cells, which makes it robust under class imbalance.

METRICS
VALUES
BARS
EQUATIONS
THEORY
LIVE PRECISION STORY
Prevalence changes the group sizes, not the rates
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 85% means the test catches about 4,250 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 20% means about 1,000 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,250 / (4,250 + 1,000) = 5,250 positive calls total — 81% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,250 positive results overall: 4,250 real positives and 1,000 false positives. Precision is 81%. Most positive results are now real cases.
Try the classic 1% example
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence.

BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.

Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.

3

BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.

F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.

NPV = negative predictive value

P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? EQUATIONS
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
PRECISION (PPV) VIA BAYES
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
Precision answers: "If the model says positive, how likely is it correct?" Rewritten via Bayes, it becomes clear that precision is not just about the model's quality (TPR and FPR) but is heavily influenced by prevalence. In a dataset where only 1% of samples are positive, even a good classifier will have many false positives drowning out the true ones. This is the base-rate fallacy in action. Increase prevalence (the Balance slider) and watch precision rise.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence. Moving the threshold left increases sensitivity but also increases false positives.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. It depends only on the negative class distribution and the chosen threshold. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. This is why accuracy alone is never sufficient. Compare it with the Balance slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. Unlike the arithmetic mean, the harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives. For asymmetric costs, consider F-beta variants.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. Unlike most other metrics, AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models. Try increasing the distance between the distribution means and watch AUC approach 1.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and is considered the most informative single metric for binary classification. It remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets because it only achieves a high score if the model performs well on both the positive and negative class.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− tells you how much a negative result reduces the odds of disease. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence, making them portable across populations with different base rates.
THE PREVALENCE PARADOX
If Prev = 0.01, TPR = 0.99, FPR = 0.01: PPV = 0.50
Even with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, half the positive predictions are wrong when the disease affects only 1% of the population. For every true positive caught, there is one false positive from the vast pool of healthy individuals. This is not a flaw in the test but a mathematical consequence of Bayes' theorem. It explains why population-wide screening for rare conditions produces so many false alarms, and why confirmatory tests exist.

THEORY
LIVE PRECISION STORY
Prevalence changes the group sizes, not the rates
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 85% means the test catches about 4,250 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 20% means about 1,000 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,250 / (4,250 + 1,000) = 5,250 positive calls total — 81% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,250 positive results overall: 4,250 real positives and 1,000 false positives. Precision is 81%. Most positive results are now real cases.
Try the classic 1% example
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence.

THEORY
LIVE PRECISION STORY
Prevalence changes the group sizes, not the rates
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 85% means the test catches about 4,250 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 20% means about 1,000 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,250 / (4,250 + 1,000) = 5,250 positive calls total — 81% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,250 positive results overall: 4,250 real positives and 1,000 false positives. Precision is 81%. Most positive results are now real cases.
Try the classic 1% example
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence.

THEORY
Click any metric card in Values to jump here. These are the standard formulas written in the usual notation.
TPR (RECALL)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
TPR = TP / (TP + FN)
Also written as: Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
Among the actual positives, what fraction did the model catch?
FPR
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
FPR = FP / (FP + TN)
Also written as: FPR = 1 - TNR
Among the actual negatives, what fraction were wrongly predicted positive?
PRECISION (PPV)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Also written as: PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Among the predicted positives, what fraction are truly positive?
ACCURACY
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
Also written as: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / N
Out of all predictions, what fraction were correct?
F1 SCORE
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
Also written as: F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall)
A balanced score that gets high only when both precision and recall are high.
AUC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
AUC = ∫01 TPR(FPR) d(FPR)
Also written as: area under the ROC curve
It summarizes performance across all thresholds, not just the current one.
NPV
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
NPV = negative predictive value
Among the predicted negatives, what fraction are truly negative?
MCC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
MCC = (TP · TN - FP · FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
Range: -1 to 1
Uses all four confusion-matrix cells, which makes it robust under class imbalance.

METRICS
VALUES
BARS
EQUATIONS
THEORY
LIVE PRECISION STORY
Prevalence changes the group sizes, not the rates
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 85% means the test catches about 4,250 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 20% means about 1,000 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,250 / (4,250 + 1,000) = 5,250 positive calls total — 81% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,250 positive results overall: 4,250 real positives and 1,000 false positives. Precision is 81%. Most positive results are now real cases.
Try the classic 1% example
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence.

THEORY
Click any metric card in Values to jump here. These are the standard formulas written in the usual notation.
TPR (RECALL)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
TPR = TP / (TP + FN)
Also written as: Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
Among the actual positives, what fraction did the model catch?
FPR
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
FPR = FP / (FP + TN)
Also written as: FPR = 1 - TNR
Among the actual negatives, what fraction were wrongly predicted positive?
PRECISION (PPV)
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Also written as: PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Among the predicted positives, what fraction are truly positive?
ACCURACY
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
Also written as: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / N
Out of all predictions, what fraction were correct?
F1 SCORE
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
Also written as: F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall)
A balanced score that gets high only when both precision and recall are high.
AUC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
AUC = ∫01 TPR(FPR) d(FPR)
Also written as: area under the ROC curve
It summarizes performance across all thresholds, not just the current one.
NPV
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
NPV = negative predictive value
Among the predicted negatives, what fraction are truly negative?
MCC
TRADITIONAL FORMULA
MCC = (TP · TN - FP · FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
Range: -1 to 1
Uses all four confusion-matrix cells, which makes it robust under class imbalance.

THEORY
LIVE PRECISION STORY
Prevalence changes the group sizes, not the rates
PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 85% means the test catches about 4,250 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 20% means about 1,000 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,250 / (4,250 + 1,000) = 5,250 positive calls total — 81% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,250 positive results overall: 4,250 real positives and 1,000 false positives. Precision is 81%. Most positive results are now real cases.
Try the classic 1% example
BAYES' THEOREM
P(D|+) = P(+|D) · P(D) / P(+)
The foundation of probabilistic classification. Given a positive test result (+), what is the probability the patient actually has the disease (D)? The answer depends on three things: how good the test is at catching true cases (likelihood), how common the disease is (prior), and how often the test fires overall (evidence). This is why a 99% accurate test can still give mostly false positives for a rare disease.
NPV VIA BAYES
NPV = TNR · (1−Prev) / (TNR · (1−Prev) + FNR · Prev)
The mirror of PPV: "If the model says negative, how likely is that correct?" When prevalence is low, most negative predictions are correct (high NPV) because negatives dominate the population. As prevalence increases, the fraction of missed positives (FN) grows relative to true negatives, and NPV drops. NPV and PPV move in opposite directions as you change prevalence, which is a key Bayesian insight.
SENSITIVITY (RECALL / TPR)
TPR = P(+|D) = TP / (TP + FN)
Of all the actual positives, how many did the model catch? A sensitivity of 0.95 means 95% of true cases are detected, but 5% are missed (false negatives). Critical in medical screening: missing a cancer diagnosis (FN) is usually worse than a false alarm (FP). Sensitivity is intrinsic to the model and threshold, not affected by prevalence.
SPECIFICITY (TNR)
TNR = P(−|D̄) = TN / (TN + FP)
Of all the actual negatives, how many did the model correctly identify? Specificity of 0.90 means 10% of healthy patients receive a false positive. Like sensitivity, specificity is independent of prevalence. High specificity is important when false positives are costly, such as unnecessary surgeries or wrongful convictions.
ACCURACY
Acc = (TP + TN) / N
The most intuitive metric: what fraction of all predictions were correct? However, accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes. A model that always predicts "negative" on a dataset with 95% negatives achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero true positives. Compare it with the Prevalence slider at extreme values to see this paradox in action.
F1 SCORE
F1 = 2 · PPV · TPR / (PPV + TPR)
The harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean punishes extreme imbalance: if either precision or recall is near zero, F1 collapses. An F1 of 0.8 guarantees that both precision and recall are at least 0.67. It is prevalence-dependent (through precision) and is most useful when you care equally about false positives and false negatives.
AUC (AREA UNDER ROC CURVE)
AUC = integral of TPR d(FPR) over [0,1]
AUC measures the model's ability to discriminate between classes across all possible thresholds. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing (diagonal ROC), AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. AUC is threshold-independent and prevalence-independent, making it ideal for comparing models.
MCC (MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT)
MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))
MCC is a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications, ranging from −1 (total disagreement) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1 and accuracy, MCC uses all four confusion matrix quadrants and remains reliable even with highly imbalanced datasets.
LIKELIHOOD RATIOS
LR+ = TPR / FPR   |   LR− = FNR / TNR
Likelihood ratios express how much a test result shifts the odds. LR+ tells you how much more likely a positive result is in a true positive vs. a false positive. LR+ > 10 is considered strong diagnostic evidence. LR− < 0.1 is strong evidence for ruling out. Unlike PPV/NPV, likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence.

PPV = TPR · Prev / (TPR · Prev + FPR · (1−Prev))
TPR is measured within positives, and FPR is measured within negatives. Changing prevalence leaves those rates alone and only changes the group sizes.
Reference cohort of 10,000 — the mosaic above uses your N slider
1

Out of 10,000 people, about 5,000 truly are positive and 5,000 truly are negative.

2

TPR 87% means the test catches about 4,352 of the 5,000 positives. TPR is measured only within the positive group — it is set by the model, not by how large that group is.

3

FPR 13% means about 648 of the 5,000 negatives are wrongly flagged. FPR is measured only within the negative group — it also does not shift when prevalence changes.

4

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4,352 / (4,352 + 648) = 5,000 positive calls total — 87% are real.

So balance did not change TPR or FPR. It changed the sizes of the two groups. That leaves about 5,000 positive results overall: 4,352 real positives and 648 false positives. Precision is 87%. Most positive results are now real cases.

Collapse all
CORE
8 metrics
›
Accuracy ↑
Higher is better
(TP + TN) / N

✓
Good for:
Overall correctness on balanced data.

✗
Watch out:
Can hide poor results on rare positives.

Precision ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
Reliable alerts; fewer false alarms.

✗
Watch out:
Can miss many positives.

Recall ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Finding positives; fewer misses.

✗
Watch out:
Can produce many false alarms.

Specificity ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FP)

✓
Good for:
Correctly clearing negative cases.

✗
Watch out:
Does not show how many positives are caught.

F1 ↑
Higher is better
2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
One score for precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Fβ ↑
Higher is better
(1 + β²) · P · R / (β² · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Choosing emphasis: β > 1 recall, β < 1 precision.

✗
Watch out:
β is not a direct error-cost ratio.

F2 ↑
Higher is better
5 · P · R / (4 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving recall more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check the false-alarm workload.

F0.5 ↑
Higher is better
1.25 · P · R / (0.25 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving precision more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check how many positives are missed.

IMBALANCE
7 metrics
›
Balanced accuracy ↑
Higher is better
(TPR + TNR) / 2

✓
Good for:
Giving both actual classes equal weight.

✗
Watch out:
Equal class weight may not fit your costs.

G-mean ↑
Higher is better
√(TPR · TNR)

✓
Good for:
Requiring both class recalls to be good.

✗
Watch out:
Zero if either class recall is zero.

Youden’s J ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance level
TPR + TNR − 1

✓
Good for:
Choosing a recall–specificity balance.

✗
Watch out:
May not select the lowest-cost cutoff.

MCC ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN − FP · FN) / √((TP + FP)(TP + FN)(TN + FP)(TN + FN))

✓
Good for:
One score using all four outcomes.

✗
Watch out:
Undefined with an empty actual or predicted class.

Cohen’s κ ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance agreement
(pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ)

✓
Good for:
Agreement beyond expected chance.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with class proportions.

Jaccard / IoU ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Overlap of predicted and true positives.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores correctly predicted negatives.

Markedness ↑
Higher is better
PPV + NPV − 1

✓
Good for:
Trust in positive and negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

ERROR RATES
8 metrics
›
FPR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (FP + TN)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among actual negatives.

✗
Watch out:
Small rates can still mean many alarms.

FNR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (FN + TP)

✓
Good for:
Misses among actual positives.

✗
Watch out:
Says nothing about false alarms.

FDR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among positive predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

FOR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Missed positives among negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Can look low when positives are rare.

NPV ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Trust in a negative prediction.

✗
Watch out:
Can look high when positives are rare.

Error rate ↓
Lower is better
(FP + FN) / N

✓
Good for:
Overall share of wrong predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Treats misses and false alarms equally.

Fowlkes–Mallows ↑
Higher is better
√(P · R)

✓
Good for:
Geometric mean of precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Diagnostic odds ratio ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN) / (FP · FN)

✓
Good for:
Summarizing test separation as an odds ratio.

✗
Watch out:
Infinite or undefined with zero FP or FN.

RANKING & PROBABILITY
5 metrics
›
ROC-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ TPR d(FPR)

✓
Good for:
Ranking positives above negatives.

✗
Watch out:
High AUC can still mean poor alert precision.

PR-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ P dR

✓
Good for:
Precision–recall tradeoffs for rare positives.

✗
Watch out:
Depends on prevalence and integration method.

Average precision ↑
Higher is better
Σₖ (Rₖ − Rₖ₋₁) · Pₖ

✓
Good for:
Precision at successive recall gains.

✗
Watch out:
AP, mAP, and trapezoidal PR-AUC differ.

Log loss ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
−mean(y · ln(p) + (1 − y) · ln(1 − p))

✓
Good for:
Scoring probabilities; penalizing confident errors.

✗
Watch out:
Confident wrong predictions get very large loss.

Brier score ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
mean((p − y)²)

✓
Good for:
Scoring squared probability errors.

✗
Watch out:
Compare with a constant-prevalence baseline.

IN PRACTICE
4 metrics
›
False alarms per hour / km ↓
Lower is better
FP / observed hours or kilometers

✓
Good for:
Estimating alarm burden over time or distance.

✗
Watch out:
Define and group alarm events consistently.

Detection latency ↓
Lower is better
t(detected) − t(event start)

✓
Good for:
Measuring how quickly detection happens.

✗
Watch out:
Report slow cases and missed events too.

Recall lower bound ↑
Higher is better
Lower confidence bound for TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Allowing for uncertainty in measured recall.

✗
Watch out:
Needs a stated method and enough test cases.

Recall per scenario ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN), within each scenario

✓
Good for:
Finding weak spots such as night or rain.

✗
Watch out:
Small groups give uncertain results.

A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 500 have the flu (yielding 480 true catches) and 500 are healthy (yielding 20 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 480 out of all 500 positive tests (96%).

Why a rare disease creates mostly false alarms. When flu is rare (10% sick), 900 of 1,000 people are healthy. A 4% false-alarm rate on 900 healthy people creates 36 false alarms, next to only 96 true catches, so Precision is 72.7%.

With the test cutoff and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

Overall Accuracy & The False Security Trap
Why accuracy alone can be dangerously deceptive on rare events
Test Accuracy: (All correct results ÷ Total)
960 out of 1,000 cases correctly classified
96%
Accuracy

Accuracy measures how often the test gives the right answer: catching flu (480 TP) plus clearing healthy people (480 TN).

⚠️ The False Security Trap: When flu is rare (e.g. 10% sick), a broken test that says "Negative" to every single patient achieves an impressive 50% accuracy—while failing to catch a single sick person (TPR = 0%)!

Skip to metrics
← CMatrixLab
Quick cheatsheet →
Print / PDF
Metrics reference

What does each score tell you? Explore simple explanations and examples from medicine, driving, fraud detection, and more.

Help me choose a metric

Choose by the decision you need to make: finding problems, reducing false alarms, keeping a review queue manageable, or trusting a predicted chance.

You do not want to miss a problem

Use recall to see how many real problems you catch. FNR tells you how many you miss.

Examples: finding an illness in a medical test, or spotting a pedestrian in front of a car. Check false alarms too, and test situations such as night or rain separately. Medical example · AEB example

You want fewer false alarms

Use precision to check how many alerts are real. FPR tells you how often normal cases get flagged.

Examples: keeping legitimate emails out of spam, avoiding wrong fraud blocks, or reducing unnecessary car warnings. Check that you still catch enough real problems. Automatic-blocking example

You want one overall score

Use accuracy for a simple count of correct predictions. If one class is much rarer, also check balanced accuracy or MCC.

Example: finding faulty parts in a factory where almost every part is good. Always look at missed defects and rejected good parts separately. Factory example

You want the most likely problems first

Use ROC-AUC to check the ordering of scores. For rare problems, PR-AUC or AP also helps show how useful the alerts are as you find more cases.

Example: putting suspicious payments at the top of a fraud review queue. Check the results for the number of payments your team can actually review. Review-queue example · Object-detection example

You need to trust the predicted chances

Use log loss or Brier score to check probability predictions.

Example: if many patients each receive a 20% risk estimate, does about 1 in 5 have the condition? A calibration plot helps you check this. Risk-score example

You care about what happens over time

Check false alarms per hour or kilometer, detection delay, and track recall.

Example: a car should spot a pedestrian quickly, keep following them, and avoid repeated false warnings. Decide what counts as one warning before measuring it. Driving-hours example · Rare-hazard example

Choose the setting that catches enough problems without causing too many false alarms. Try a scenario in the calculator ↓

secondary.text:
CMatrixLab
by Martin Grossman
martin.grossman@gmail.com
Generic ML
Reset ↺

Your flu test is positive. What’s the chance you really have flu? That’s precision—and it also depends on how common flu is among the people tested.
Compare 10% and 50% sick using the same test. Precision changes, even though the share of sick people correctly testing positive (TPR) and the share of people without flu getting a false alarm (FPR) stay the same.

32 of 32 metrics

Collapse all
CORE
8 metrics
›
Accuracy ↑
Higher is better
(TP + TN) / N

✓
Good for:
Overall correctness on balanced data.

✗
Watch out:
Can hide poor results on rare positives.

Precision ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
Reliable alerts; fewer false alarms.

✗
Watch out:
Can miss many positives.

Recall ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Finding positives; fewer misses.

✗
Watch out:
Can produce many false alarms.

Specificity ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FP)

✓
Good for:
Correctly clearing negative cases.

✗
Watch out:
Does not show how many positives are caught.

F1 ↑
Higher is better
2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
One score for precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Fβ ↑
Higher is better
(1 + β²) · P · R / (β² · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Choosing emphasis: β > 1 recall, β < 1 precision.

✗
Watch out:
β is not a direct error-cost ratio.

F2 ↑
Higher is better
5 · P · R / (4 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving recall more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check the false-alarm workload.

F0.5 ↑
Higher is better
1.25 · P · R / (0.25 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving precision more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check how many positives are missed.

IMBALANCE
7 metrics
›
Balanced accuracy ↑
Higher is better
(TPR + TNR) / 2

✓
Good for:
Giving both actual classes equal weight.

✗
Watch out:
Equal class weight may not fit your costs.

G-mean ↑
Higher is better
√(TPR · TNR)

✓
Good for:
Requiring both class recalls to be good.

✗
Watch out:
Zero if either class recall is zero.

Youden’s J ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance level
TPR + TNR − 1

✓
Good for:
Choosing a recall–specificity balance.

✗
Watch out:
May not select the lowest-cost cutoff.

MCC ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN − FP · FN) / √((TP + FP)(TP + FN)(TN + FP)(TN + FN))

✓
Good for:
One score using all four outcomes.

✗
Watch out:
Undefined with an empty actual or predicted class.

Cohen’s κ ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance agreement
(pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ)

✓
Good for:
Agreement beyond expected chance.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with class proportions.

Jaccard / IoU ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Overlap of predicted and true positives.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores correctly predicted negatives.

Markedness ↑
Higher is better
PPV + NPV − 1

✓
Good for:
Trust in positive and negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

ERROR RATES
8 metrics
›
FPR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (FP + TN)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among actual negatives.

✗
Watch out:
Small rates can still mean many alarms.

FNR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (FN + TP)

✓
Good for:
Misses among actual positives.

✗
Watch out:
Says nothing about false alarms.

FDR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among positive predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

FOR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Missed positives among negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Can look low when positives are rare.

NPV ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Trust in a negative prediction.

✗
Watch out:
Can look high when positives are rare.

Error rate ↓
Lower is better
(FP + FN) / N

✓
Good for:
Overall share of wrong predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Treats misses and false alarms equally.

Fowlkes–Mallows ↑
Higher is better
√(P · R)

✓
Good for:
Geometric mean of precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Diagnostic odds ratio ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN) / (FP · FN)

✓
Good for:
Summarizing test separation as an odds ratio.

✗
Watch out:
Infinite or undefined with zero FP or FN.

RANKING & PROBABILITY
5 metrics
›
ROC-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ TPR d(FPR)

✓
Good for:
Ranking positives above negatives.

✗
Watch out:
High AUC can still mean poor alert precision.

PR-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ P dR

✓
Good for:
Precision–recall tradeoffs for rare positives.

✗
Watch out:
Depends on prevalence and integration method.

Average precision ↑
Higher is better
Σₖ (Rₖ − Rₖ₋₁) · Pₖ

✓
Good for:
Precision at successive recall gains.

✗
Watch out:
AP, mAP, and trapezoidal PR-AUC differ.

Log loss ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
−mean(y · ln(p) + (1 − y) · ln(1 − p))

✓
Good for:
Scoring probabilities; penalizing confident errors.

✗
Watch out:
Confident wrong predictions get very large loss.

Brier score ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
mean((p − y)²)

✓
Good for:
Scoring squared probability errors.

✗
Watch out:
Compare with a constant-prevalence baseline.

IN PRACTICE
4 metrics
›
False alarms per hour / km ↓
Lower is better
FP / observed hours or kilometers

✓
Good for:
Estimating alarm burden over time or distance.

✗
Watch out:
Define and group alarm events consistently.

Detection latency ↓
Lower is better
t(detected) − t(event start)

✓
Good for:
Measuring how quickly detection happens.

✗
Watch out:
Report slow cases and missed events too.

Recall lower bound ↑
Higher is better
Lower confidence bound for TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Allowing for uncertainty in measured recall.

✗
Watch out:
Needs a stated method and enough test cases.

Recall per scenario ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN), within each scenario

✓
Good for:
Finding weak spots such as night or rain.

✗
Watch out:
Small groups give uncertain results.

ROC & Trade-offs
A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 500 have the flu (yielding 480 true catches) and 500 are healthy (yielding 20 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 480 out of all 500 positive tests (96%).

Why a rare disease creates mostly false alarms. When flu is rare (10% sick), 900 of 1,000 people are healthy. A 4% false-alarm rate on 900 healthy people creates 36 false alarms, next to only 96 true catches, so Precision is 72.7%.

With the test cutoff and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

Overall Accuracy & The False Security Trap
Why accuracy alone can be dangerously deceptive on rare events
Test Accuracy: (All correct results ÷ Total)
960 out of 1,000 cases correctly classified
96%
Accuracy

Accuracy measures how often the test gives the right answer: catching flu (480 TP) plus clearing healthy people (480 TN).

⚠️ The False Security Trap: When flu is rare (e.g. 10% sick), a broken test that says "Negative" to every single patient achieves an impressive 50% accuracy—while failing to catch a single sick person (TPR = 0%)!

What does each score tell you? Explore simple explanations and examples from medicine, driving, fraud detection, and more.

Help me choose a metric

Choose by the decision you need to make: finding problems, reducing false alarms, keeping a review queue manageable, or trusting a predicted chance.

You do not want to miss a problem

Use recall to see how many real problems you catch. FNR tells you how many you miss.

Examples: finding an illness in a medical test, or spotting a pedestrian in front of a car. Check false alarms too, and test situations such as night or rain separately. Medical example · AEB example

You want fewer false alarms

Use precision to check how many alerts are real. FPR tells you how often normal cases get flagged.

Examples: keeping legitimate emails out of spam, avoiding wrong fraud blocks, or reducing unnecessary car warnings. Check that you still catch enough real problems. Automatic-blocking example

You want one overall score

Use accuracy for a simple count of correct predictions. If one class is much rarer, also check balanced accuracy or MCC.

Example: finding faulty parts in a factory where almost every part is good. Always look at missed defects and rejected good parts separately. Factory example

You want the most likely problems first

Use ROC-AUC to check the ordering of scores. For rare problems, PR-AUC or AP also helps show how useful the alerts are as you find more cases.

Example: putting suspicious payments at the top of a fraud review queue. Check the results for the number of payments your team can actually review. Review-queue example · Object-detection example

You need to trust the predicted chances

Use log loss or Brier score to check probability predictions.

Example: if many patients each receive a 20% risk estimate, does about 1 in 5 have the condition? A calibration plot helps you check this. Risk-score example

You care about what happens over time

Check false alarms per hour or kilometer, detection delay, and track recall.

Example: a car should spot a pedestrian quickly, keep following them, and avoid repeated false warnings. Decide what counts as one warning before measuring it. Driving-hours example · Rare-hazard example

Choose the setting that catches enough problems without causing too many false alarms. Try a scenario in the calculator ↓

Bayes’ theorem: from a positive test to the chance of flu

Start with how common flu is (prior p = 50%). Then combine true detections (TPR) and false alarms (FPR) to find the posterior probability P(flu | test +).

Bayes’ theorem in rate form

The bar | means “given”. TPR and FPR condition on the actual group (P(test + | flu) and P(test + | no flu)), while Precision flips the condition to ask about a positive result (P(flu | test +)).

0.96 × 0.5 ÷ [0.96 × 0.5 + 0.04 × 0.5] = 96%

The same precision as in the graph, calculated from TPR, FPR, and the prior p.

Bayes’ theorem in 3 natural steps: from 1,000 people to your chance of flu

The easiest way to understand Bayes’ theorem is with 1,000 people: first split them by how common flu is (p = 50%), next count how many from each row get a Test +, and finally take the sick share of all positive tests (P(flu | test +)).

Why the 1,000-person count formula equals Bayes’ formula

The vertical bar | means “given” (which group we restrict our attention to). Because TP = 1,000 × TPR × p and FP = 1,000 × FPR × (1 − p), the population size 1,000 cancels out from top and bottom—turning expected counts into Bayes’ exact rate formula for P(flu | test +).

0.96 × 0.5 ÷ [0.96 × 0.5 + 0.04 × 0.5] = 96%

Positive Likelihood Ratio (LR+ = TPR ÷ FPR): 24×. Dividing TP by FP gives Posterior Odds = LR+ × Prior Odds.

6282606.what: Dense light/colorblind/dark-capable dashboard with direct TPR/FPR/prevalence controls, linked Gaussian-score mode, matrix/mosaic, metric values/bars/equations/theory, distribution curves/top view, and ROC.
6282606.difference: Adds CSV/JSON upload over the mosaic-focused predecessor. The 1,500-row CSV test loaded only 1,000 rows; a three-row JSON file loaded successfully.
6282606.use: Reference for the first importer and empirical score/ROC workflow.
6282606.caution: At 390px the dashboard becomes a long scrolling document (~2,177px measured), unlike the later mobile tabbed rework.

9503516.what: Dark manual-rate dashboard with panel reordering, live equations, matrix, score cards, presets, counts/rates, ROC and PR.
9503516.difference: Root HTML is byte-identical to old_movable and old_Release_Dark_Claude. Width button changes the equations panel (rather than a width control on every panel). Reordering and refresh persistence worked.
9503516.use: Reference for the original simpler reorder/width persistence implementation.
9503516.caution: The root HTML is an identical homepage snapshot, but this branch also has a separate /dev/index.html, so the whole branch is not identical to every alias.

4ad5b18.what: Most complete compact CMatrixLab: five domains (Medical, Car braking, Spam, Fraud, Generic ML), Default/4-Up/Gaussians/ROC/PR/Bayes views, three matrix arrangements, linked score dots and matrix markers, group dragging, and separate Learn/Reference/Cheatsheet pages.
4ad5b18.difference: Latest checkpoint of the compact line. Defaults to medical prevalence 10%. Improves drag sensitivity, axis correction and the hand-shaped drag hint relative to Branch_1e973a51. It does not include real-data import or movable dashboard panels.
4ad5b18.use: Continue the learning-focused product here; address the existing detailed QA report before release.
4ad5b18.caution: The previous complete QA report records F1-edge, explanation, accessibility and responsive issues. Opening successfully here is not a clean release certification.

1e973a5.what: Same broad five-domain/six-view experience and separate educational/reference pages as the latest compact version. Group dragging adjusts separation horizontally or positive proportion vertically.
1e973a5.difference: Earlier drag implementation locks the initial axis. A gesture that began horizontally remained at separation 63%, prevalence 10%; the same gesture in the latest branch reset separation to 60% and changed prevalence to 18%.
1e973a5.use: Useful comparison point for the drag behavior; not a separate product direction.
1e973a5.caution: Local-only branch name. Latest compact branch is its verified descendant.

a0af2f9.what: Flu/Generic ML simulator with threshold, separation, positive-share controls, matching dot/square markers and three metric buttons (TPR, FPR, Precision). Hover/click highlighting and pin behavior are present.
a0af2f9.difference: Adds interactive metric highlighting to the earlier threshold-dragging version. No scenario dropdown, six-view graph tabs or Learn panel. Medical starts at 50% positives.
a0af2f9.use: Small, focused base-rate and linked-highlight demonstration.
a0af2f9.caution: simple and feature_simple_hover_metrics are exactly the same commit, not two distinct implementations.

a9c5545.what: Minimal flu/Generic ML simulator with the blue draggable threshold line, two linked displays, three headline rates, 10%/50% share shortcuts and Reset.
a9c5545.difference: Threshold dragging works in the browser. The later metric-card pinning/hover feature is absent.
a9c5545.use: Reference for the initial graph-handle interaction.
a9c5545.caution: Superseded by the hover/story/current compact line; no real-data upload or movable panels.

c640622.what: The homepage redirects to cmatrixlab_minimal_readable.html. It presents a basic flu/Generic ML explanation, sliders, score dots, confusion matrix and precision strip.
c640622.difference: This is the initial minimal readable version. The inspected page does not expose the later threshold-drag handle or interactive metric-card buttons; use the sliders. Defaults to 50% sick share.
c640622.use: Historical baseline for how the compact teaching experience began.
c640622.caution: The real page is the redirect target, not the tiny root index.html.

7db2c1b.what: Builds on the simple highlight simulator and adds Learn more with four sections: Basics, Formulas, Bayes and Trade-offs. Learning content and live model remain in the same page.
7db2c1b.difference: The Bayes tab displays prior/evidence/posterior counts and 10%/50% comparison cards. It does not yet add duplicate sliders inside the Bayes section.
7db2c1b.use: Reference for the inline learning flow and early explanation copy.
7db2c1b.caution: No multi-domain scenario dropdown or dashboard graph-view strip.

b37face.role: Expanded Bayes lesson and visual refinement
b37face.what: Keeps the compact simulator plus inline four-tab learning layer, with clearer natural-frequency Bayes steps, conditional-probability explanations and live equations.
b37face.difference: Compared with feature_simple_bayes_story, the Bayes tab adds its own synchronized threshold, separation and prevalence sliders. Browser inspection found six visible inputs there (three main plus three Bayes) versus three in the earlier branch.
b37face.use: Useful source for inline educational controls and Bayes explanation layout.
b37face.caution: Still the two-domain/one-main-graph generation, not the modern five-domain/six-view dashboard.

40918b1.what: Advanced direct-rate/Gaussian dashboard with matrix/mosaic, linked metric highlights, equations and theory panels, class-distribution views and ROC.
40918b1.difference: Focuses on mosaic presentation and larger labels. It has no custom-data file input. Its default manual rates are 90% TPR / 10% FPR rather than the later imported-data line’s 85% / 20%.
40918b1.use: Reference for mosaic readability and metric-to-outcome highlighting.
40918b1.caution: Older long mobile layout; later branches carry broader data and model features.

8facffd.what: Real-data dashboard with the same major manual/Gaussian, matrix/mosaic, metric/theory, ROC and distribution tools as the custom-data line.
8facffd.difference: Increases CSV/JSON capacity to 2,000 rows in source/UI. The browser test successfully imported all 1,500 supplied rows.
8facffd.use: Useful source for the larger import cap and uploaded-score workflow.
8facffd.caution: Despite the name, the built-in simulator still starts at N=1,000; the changed limit concerns uploaded records. Phone layout remains long.

e54de22.role: Similar UI with reduced import cap
e54de22.what: Visually close to custom_data_2000, with the same direct-rate/Gaussian switches, matrix/mosaic and educational metric panels.
e54de22.difference: The actual diff against custom_data_2000 changes five limits/labels from 2,000 to 1,000, including maximum dots; it does not introduce a distinct new homepage bounds control. Browser import loaded 1,000 of 1,500 records.
e54de22.use: Keep as a historical comparison for the 1,000-row/dot-limit behavior.
e54de22.caution: Do not infer the feature from the branch name: the measurable difference is the lower cap.

fea3eda.what: Retains the advanced dashboard and real-data importer, but extracts numerical/import/ROC functions into metrics_core.js and includes unit and visual-test scaffolding.
fea3eda.difference: The browser loaded metrics_core.js successfully; matrix/mosaic, all metric views, model-mode switch and CSV/JSON imports worked. Its CSV cap remains 1,000.
fea3eda.use: Best branch to study for separating the advanced app’s math from rendering and testing it independently.
fea3eda.caution: Not the newest UI. The full historical test suite was not run during this comparison campaign; presence of tests is not a claim that every test passed.

4d301a2.role: Default remote branch; broad data feature set
4d301a2.what: The remote default is master. It is the advanced Plotly dashboard with themes, real CSV/JSON input, manual/linked score modes, matrix/mosaic, values/bars/equations/theory and distribution/ROC tools.
4d301a2.difference: Compared with refactor_big, prototypes move under archive/, the index returns to a large standalone implementation and metrics_core.js/test scaffolding disappear. The UI allows 2,000 upload rows; 1,500 were imported in the browser.
4d301a2.use: Useful broad advanced desktop baseline; it is not the compact simulator currently checked out.
4d301a2.caution: 390px homepage requires long scrolling. Default remote branch status does not mean it is the newest teaching-focused implementation.

1f35d26.what: Keeps the advanced desktop/data dashboard but reworks phones into pinned manual controls and Matrix / Metrics / Curves / ROC tabs. Advanced tools reveal data/model options.
1f35d26.difference: At 390×844 the default document fits the viewport and each of the four mobile tabs activated its intended panel. Advanced reveals the Custom data entry and Manual/Gaussian switch. Both 1,500-row CSV and three-row JSON imports worked.
1f35d26.use: Preferred advanced branch for phone-oriented data exploration; good source for a tabbed mobile layout.
1f35d26.caution: The manual ROC point can sit off the Gaussian ROC curve by design; the UI explicitly warns about the two modes. Phone targets and all numerical boundaries were not exhaustively audited here.

ffb6fc5.what: A different advanced workflow: Step 1 shapes the two class distributions; Step 2 chooses the operating point; Step 3 sets N and prevalence. Direct/linked modes connect distributions, threshold and rates.
ffb6fc5.difference: Includes collapsible instructional sections, weighted Gaussian distributions, ROC, matrix/mosaic and metric views. Phone layout adds a tune/inspect/compare summary and Controls / Outcomes / Metrics / Distributions navigation. Defaults to linked mode.
ffb6fc5.use: Good reference for the clearest “shape → threshold → population” interaction sequence.
ffb6fc5.caution: Long desktop/mobile document (about 1,034 / 2,768px in the initial check). No real-data file input was exposed on the root page.

04bef33.what: Shows explicit direct-vs-linked mode messaging, Gaussian means/spreads, dataset size and threshold, confusion-matrix/mosaic views, metrics and theory, and ROC/distribution charts.
04bef33.difference: Earlier generation with 90% TPR / 10% FPR defaults, more controls visible at once and fewer separated metric presentation buttons than later custom-data branches.
04bef33.use: Historical comparison for the transition from direct-rate tiles to Gaussian-score modeling.
04bef33.caution: Both desktop and phone pages scroll; no CSV/JSON importer on this root page.

3c2e276.role: Movable panels with widths on every tile
3c2e276.what: Dark manual-rate playground with N/prevalence/TPR/FPR, live equations, matrix, derived metrics, preset buttons, counts/rates charts, ROC/likelihood-ratio and PR panels.
3c2e276.difference: Panel drag reorder and per-panel width buttons (1x→2x etc.) work, with order/sizes surviving refresh. Its root homepage is byte-identical to old_dev.
3c2e276.use: Best existing source if the requirement is movable dashboard tiles with per-panel width changes.
3c2e276.caution: The root uses internal scrolling on phones; “no document overflow” does not mean every panel fits. /dev/index.html is only a placeholder with a missing stylesheet (404).

7d53851.role: Same root as main; working nested development app
7d53851.what: Same dark movable, resizable-by-width-button dashboard at the root as main. Panel reorder, width change and refresh persistence all worked.
7d53851.difference: Changes are in dev/index.html, dev/index.css, dev/js/app.js and styles/mosaic.css. Unlike main/dev’s heading-only placeholder, /dev/index.html is a complete working dashboard.
7d53851.use: Reference for the modular nested development experiment and movable-tile behavior.
7d53851.caution: Nested development screenshot shows dense panels, scrolling and clipped/overflowing inner text; it needs layout work before reuse.

ce97d3a.what: Same dark manual-rate movable dashboard and equation-width control as old_Release and old_movable.
ce97d3a.difference: Identical root index.html hash and rendered controls to those two branches; browser reorder, width change and refresh persistence all passed.
ce97d3a.use: Historical snapshot; no unique homepage capability was found.
ce97d3a.caution: The name suggests a separate dark redesign, but the actual root page is identical to the other two listed versions.

9a7762a.what: Dark classifier dashboard whose grips reorder tiles and whose Width button cycles the equations tile width.
9a7762a.difference: Root matches both old release variants. Moving Parameters after the matrix changed order, persisted after refresh, and Width changed class tile→tile span2.
9a7762a.use: Smallest older source to inspect for drag ordering and persisted equation width.
9a7762a.caution: This is button-based width/span resizing, not arbitrary corner-handle resizing.

5176eb1.what: Dark manual-rate classifier playground with parameters, matrix, derived metrics, presets, count/rate charts, ROC/PR and live equations.
5176eb1.difference: No Edit Layout controls were exposed. A literal code-fence marker is visible in body text, and the desktop screenshot has uneven spacing and native-looking controls compared with later dark versions.
5176eb1.caution: Not a recommended implementation base; newer dark snapshots are more coherent and add real layout controls.
